title: Emerging Research Fronts in Public Relations Scholarship: An Analytical Synthesis of Technological Disruption, Epistemic Diversification, and Disciplinary Self-Examination
content: This paper presents an analytical synthesis of contemporary research fronts in public relations (PR) scholarship, drawing on recent work in leading journals (Public Relations Review, Journal of Public Relations Research, Corporate Communications: An International Journal), agenda-setting signals from disciplinary bodies (ICA, IPR, PRSA), and 2025–2026 special-issue programs. Seven interrelated research fronts are identified: (a) artificial intelligence adoption, ethics, and disciplinary disruption; (b) disinformation, trust, and organizational resilience; (c) theoretical and methodological pluralism, including de-Westernization; (d) employee communication, advocacy, and internal activism; (e) crisis spillover and contagion; (f) measurement, evaluation, and predictive analytics; and (g) bibliometric self-mapping. The analysis argues that these fronts are shaped by three macro-level forces—technological disruption, epistemic diversification, and disciplinary self-examination—and that the intersections among them constitute the field’s most promising publication spaces. Drawing on recent empirical evidence, including a 277-agency survey of AI adoption across the Arab world (Koa et al., 2025), a longitudinal analysis of 630 fact-checks of disinformation targeting organizations in Spain (Rodríguez Fernández et al., 2026), and a dedicated special issue on crisis spillover (Laufer & Wang, 2024), the synthesis shows that the field’s most successful emerging work does not abandon established PR theory but redeploys it in new empirical territories. The paper concludes with a maturity–opportunity assessment and a strategic map of research gaps to guide manuscript positioning in Q1/Q2 outlets during the 2026–2027 publication cycle.
